The proof concerns undirected simple graphs and ordinary perfect matching, not directed flows, residual capacities, or antiparallel arcs. No identity analogous to the refuted residual-flow identity is used.

No step selects a first vertex of a componentwise symmetric difference of two paths. The target's symmetric difference is solely the standard edge-set distance, while the splice paths are explicitly constructed.

The parent never deletes a spanning tree or assumes that a tree crosses a cut once. The connected splice only uses the valid fact that connectivity supplies an edge between the current union of factor cycles and its nonempty complement.
No local colorings are glued into a global coloring. The Hamiltonian cycle is built as one explicit global witness, so the record's local-to-global incompatibility does not arise.
The proof defines neither maximal common subgraphs nor graph intersection via a universal maximality predicate. Its only set operation of this kind is ordinary edge-set symmetric difference.
No weighted graph, minimum spanning tree, or inference from MST membership to bridgehood appears in any load-bearing claim.
The argument uses neither chordal graphs nor decomposition by clique pasting, so the complete-graph obstruction in this record is irrelevant.

Although the splice conceptually orients factor paths, it does not claim arbitrary added orientations preserve a longest-path bound. It directly exhibits a spanning cycle, and additional graph edges cannot invalidate that witness.
Connectivity is used as an ordinary graph property and can be tested by standard traversal; the proof never characterizes it using a single adjacency-matrix power.
No electrical-network quantity, effective resistance, or distance-over-degree inequality is used.
The proof contains no river-crossing instance or claimed one-crossing equivalence with Vertex Cover.
No reduction from Vertex Cover to a ferrying problem is present, so the claw counterexample does not meet the hypotheses of any claim.
No ferry-capacity bound is converted into a coloring or partition bound. The component counts here come directly from vertex-disjoint cycles and exact cardinality inequalities.

The proof never infers a length-k path from minimum degree k−1 or uses the refuted induction. Minimum degree appears only in a valid low-degree isolation edit and in the complete-bipartite barrier family.
There is no induction over forest components and no assertion that an odd-order component supports an all-odd-degree spanning subgraph.
No pruning order is used and no bound on remaining degree is transferred to degree toward previously deleted vertices.
The construction does not recursively freeze a minimum spanning tree or use edge weights; the fan-graph MST failure is unrelated.
No radix sort or stability argument occurs in the proof.

The auxiliary perfect-matching graph may be larger than G, but it has polynomial size and is only an internal computation. Runtime is therefore polynomial in the original n, while the edit radius is correctly measured on the returned graph's unchanged n-vertex set; no approximation exponent is transferred across sizes.
No inductive boundary-complexity recurrence or rectangle-union argument appears.
No preorder, linear-order extension, or empty-family intersection is used.

The connected splice is not a spanning-tree exchange. Its edge xy joins two vertex-disjoint factor cycles and hence cannot be one of their cycle edges; the parent makes no unsupported claim that an exchange edge lies outside an arbitrary second tree.
The proof concerns undirected Hamiltonian cycles, not directed transitive reductions or acyclicity.

final_writeup:
The universal statement remains unresolved here for c>3. A complete polynomial-time construction is proved for every 0<c≤3. More generally, the construction works whenever a computable 2-factor has sufficiently few components; this settles, for arbitrary c, all graphs of girth at least c. Cheap non-Hamiltonicity edits are also obtained from component-count obstructions, including every graph having a vertex of degree at most n/c.

The central unresolved case is therefore a connected graph with minimum degree greater than n/c, no readily exposed component obstruction, and only 2-factors having too many components for the elementary splice. A precise sufficient reduction is given: producing, on every Hamiltonian graph, some 2-factor with o(n) components would settle all fixed c.

The threshold 3 is sharp for the elementary low-degree-versus-Hamiltonian-completion dichotomy. For every c>3 there are imbalanced complete bipartite graphs whose minimum degree and distance to every Hamiltonian graph both exceed n/c. They are nevertheless correctly handled by a stronger non-Hamiltonicity certificate, so this is a barrier to the proof method rather than a counterexample to the target.

results.claim: Existence of a 2-factor, and an explicit 2-factor when one exists, can be determined in polynomial time.
results.proof_sketch: For each vertex v of degree d(v), create one incidence vertex (v,e) for every incident edge e and d(v)−2 private dummy vertices; if d(v)<2, no 2-factor exists. Join every private dummy to every incidence vertex belonging to v. For each original edge e=uv, join (u,e) to (v,e). A perfect matching in this polynomial-size auxiliary graph matches exactly d(v)−2 incidences at v to its dummies, leaving exactly two incidences matched across original-edge links. Those links form a 2-factor. Conversely, any 2-factor extends to such a perfect matching by matching all unused incidences bijectively to the private dummies. Thus a polynomial general-graph perfect-matching algorithm supplies the required routine.

results.claim: If the 2-factor routine reports that none exists, returning (G,nil) is correct.
results.proof_sketch: Every Hamiltonian cycle is itself a spanning 2-regular subgraph, hence a 2-factor. Therefore absence of a 2-factor implies that G is non-Hamiltonian.

results.claim: If G has a 2-factor with q cycle components, one can add at most q edges and explicitly obtain a Hamiltonian cycle; if G is connected, at most q−1 additions suffice.
results.proof_sketch: For the q-edge bound, break one edge conceptually in every factor cycle, orient the resulting spanning paths, and connect their terminal endpoints cyclically. Add only connectors absent from G; the broken factor edges need not actually be deleted. For the connected bound, maintain a cycle D spanning some factor components. Connectivity supplies an original edge xy from D to an unmerged factor cycle C. Choose cycle edges xx′ of D and yy′ of C. Replacing these two edges in the witness by the existing edge xy and the edge x′y′ merges D and C; only x′y′ may need adding. Repeating costs at most one addition per merge.

results.claim: For every fixed real 0<c≤3, Sidestep(Hamiltonian Cycle,dist_e,n/c) is in FP.
results.proof_sketch: Handle n<3 directly. If G is disconnected, output (G,nil). Otherwise compute a 2-factor; if none exists, use the preceding nil result. Its q components are simple cycles of length at least three, so q≤n/3. Merge them as above, adding at most q−1≤n/3≤n/c edges, and output the resulting graph and explicit Hamiltonian cycle. All operations are polynomial and preserve the labeled vertex set.

results.claim: For arbitrary fixed c>0, the target is polynomially solvable on graphs whose girth is at least c.
results.proof_sketch: Test connectivity and compute a 2-factor as above, using nil if either necessary condition fails. If a factor exists and the girth is g≥c, each factor component has at least g vertices, so q≤n/g≤n/c. The splice construction therefore stays within the required radius. In particular, the result holds on triangle-free graphs for every c≤4.

results.claim: A general cheap non-Hamiltonicity edit is obtained from a component-count obstruction.
results.proof_sketch: Let S⊆V and partition V\S into p nonempty parts P_1,…,P_p with p>max{1,|S|}. Delete every edge having endpoints in two different parts, and suppose at most n/c edges are deleted. In the resulting H, H−S has at least p components. Removing a nonempty k-vertex set from a Hamiltonian cycle leaves at most k path components; with S empty, the cycle remains connected. Hence H cannot be Hamiltonian, and (H,nil) is a valid output.

results.claim: For every c, any graph with a vertex of degree at most n/c admits a polynomial-time valid nil output within radius n/c.
results.proof_sketch: For n≥2, delete all edges incident with such a vertex v. This uses deg(v)≤n/c edits and isolates v, so the resulting graph is disconnected and non-Hamiltonian. The finitely many smaller conventions are handled directly.

results.claim: A sublinear-component 2-factor routine would settle the full target for every fixed c.
results.proof_sketch: Suppose a polynomial routine returns a 2-factor on every graph having one and, whenever G is Hamiltonian, its returned factor has at most b(n)=o(n) components. Fix c and choose a constant N so that b(n)−1≤n/c for n≥N. Handle n<N by exhaustive search, which is constant work for fixed c. For n≥N, merge the returned q-component factor when q−1≤n/c. If q−1>n/c, the promised guarantee implies contrapositively that G is non-Hamiltonian, so return (G,nil). Thus finding such a routine is a precisely isolated sufficient step for the unresolved radii.

results.claim: For every c>3, high minimum degree alone cannot guarantee a Hamiltonian graph within n/c edits.
results.proof_sketch: Choose a rational α with 1/c<α<(1−1/c)/2 and infinitely many n for which a=αn is integral; put b=n−a and G=K_{a,b}. Then δ(G)=a>n/c. In any cyclic ordering let x and z be the numbers of consecutive B-B and A-A pairs. Counting incidences gives x−z=b−a, so at least b−a nonedges occur. Conversely, separating a nonempty B-blocks by the a vertices of A realizes exactly b−a nonedges. Hence the distance from G to the set of Hamiltonian graphs is b−a=(1−2α)n>n/c. G itself is certified non-Hamiltonian because its bipartition is imbalanced.

results.claim: The n/3 component bound for an arbitrary 2-factor remains tight even under the promise that the graph is Hamiltonian.
results.proof_sketch: For n=3q, q≥2, take q disjoint vertex triples and include every triangle edge inside each triple. Also add a Hamiltonian cycle that visits the triples in an interleaved order, so consecutive vertices always belong to different triples. The graph is Hamiltonian but contains the triangle factor with exactly q=n/3 components. Therefore an extension past c=3 must choose a more informative factor or exploit a stronger no-certificate; the mere existence of an arbitrary 2-factor cannot improve the bound.
